BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- Timothy Connick was in agony for six years. In bed at night, it felt as if a pair of scissors was sticking out of his foot. "I turn over, and it's just like they're getting jammed in more." Timothy Connick got relief from chronic pain through a peripheral nerve stimulator implanted above his hip. Connick, 52 from Lynn, Massachusetts, injured his foot falling from a loading dock at work 11 years ago. "I fell about seven feet onto the concrete and smashed my heel. It started hurting that moment and kept hurting for six years after that." Connick is among millions. As many as one in three American adults suffer from chronic pain, according to the American Chronic Pain Association. The organization defines chronic pain as "pain that continues a month or more beyond the usual recovery period for an injury or illness or that goes on for months or years because of a chronic condition."  It's usually not constant, the group says, but can disrupt the sufferer's life. Over the years, Connick consulted multiple doctors and tried two dozen medications for pain management, but nothing eased the pain and the resulting depression. "It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there," he recalls. He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," she says. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients." Oaklander sees many patients whom she describes as "bouncing around the health care system" for years with no firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups. "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she says. "The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day." Much more difficult, she says, is the second group: "Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury." Connick falls in the second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays show broken bones, but not nerve damage. "It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," she said.  Health Minute: The struggle of managing chronic pain » . Oaklander says pain medications can help most patients, but there are other options. For instance, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice. In Connick's case, relief came through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. Based on pacemaker technology, the stimulator is placed under the skin and works by giving off benign pulses that override pain signals to the brain, Oaklander explains. She cautions that minor surgery is involved, and the device works in only about half the patients who get it. For Connick, it made all the difference. "The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn't been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away." These days, Connick is back at work loading trucks. He's on his feet all day and doesn't complain about any pain. Oaklander concludes: "If you have chronic pain, don't take no for an answer....I think it's important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to." E-mail to a friend . Judy Fortin is a correspondent with CNN Medical News. Linda Ciampa of Accent Health contributed to this report.

**BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)** — For six grueling years, Timothy Connick lived in unrelenting agony. At night, the sensation in his foot was excruciating—as if a pair of scissors were plunging into his flesh. 

"I turn over, and it's just like they're getting jammed in more," Connick recalls. 

Connick, a 52-year-old resident of Lynn, Massachusetts, sustained the injury eleven years ago after falling seven feet from a loading dock onto concrete, shattering his heel. "It started hurting that moment and kept hurting for six years after that."

Connick’s ordeal is far from unique. According to the American Chronic Pain Association, up to one in three American adults suffers from chronic pain. The organization defines the condition as "pain that continues a month or more beyond the usual recovery period for an injury or illness or that goes on for months or years because of a chronic condition." Although the pain is not always constant, the association notes that its impact can severely disrupt a sufferer's life.

Over the years, Connick consulted numerous physicians and tried two dozen pain management medications, yet nothing alleviated the relentless discomfort or the debilitating depression that followed. "It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there," he recalls.

His trajectory finally changed when he was referred to neurologist Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, Director of the Nerve Injury Unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston.

"Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," Dr. Oaklander explains. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients." Consequently, she frequently sees patients who have spent years "bouncing around the health care system" without a definitive diagnosis.

Dr. Oaklander divides chronic pain sufferers into two distinct categories: "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she says, citing arthritis patients who experience daily joint pain as a classic example. The far more challenging category, she notes, comprises "patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury."

Connick fell into this second, more complex category. While X-rays clearly revealed his shattered bones, they were incapable of detecting nerve damage. "It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," Dr. Oaklander notes.

While pain medications offer relief for many patients, Dr. Oaklander emphasizes that alternative options exist. For instance, if the pain stems from an orthopedic issue, physical therapy may be the most effective course of treatment. In Connick's case, however, lasting relief arrived through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. 

Based on cardiac pacemaker technology, the subcutaneous device emits benign electrical pulses that override pain signals before they reach the brain. Dr. Oaklander cautions that the procedure involves minor surgery and proves effective in only about half of the patients who receive it.

For Connick, however, the device was life-changing. "The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn't been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away."

Today, Connick has successfully returned to his job loading trucks. He spends his entire workday on his feet without a single complaint of pain.

Reflecting on Connick's journey, Dr. Oaklander offers crucial advice to others: "If you have chronic pain, don't take no for an answer.... I think it's important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to."

***

*CNN Medical News correspondent Judy Fortin and Linda Ciampa of Accent Health contributed to this report.*

### Navigating the Shadows of Chronic Pain: Systemic Gaps and the Path to Relief

Chronic pain is one of the most pervasive yet misunderstood health crises in the United States today. According to health estimates, up to one in three American adults suffers from chronic pain—defined clinically as pain that persists for a month or more beyond the normal recovery period, or continues for years due to an ongoing condition. For millions, this is not merely a temporary discomfort, but a life-altering condition that affects every aspect of daily existence. 

Despite its prevalence, the journey to finding effective treatment is often long and demoralizing. A vast number of chronic pain sufferers spend years bouncing around the healthcare system, moving from specialist to specialist without receiving a firm diagnosis or appropriate care. This systemic issue is largely driven by a significant gap in medical training. Ironically, while pain is the primary reason patients seek medical care in the first place, historical deficiencies in medical school curriculums have left many healthcare providers feeling severely unprepared to diagnose and treat complex chronic pain conditions. 

The human toll of this medical blind spot is illustrated by the story of Timothy Connick. For six agonizing years, Connick suffered from debilitating chronic foot pain. In his desperate search for answers, he consulted numerous doctors and was prescribed roughly two dozen different medications. None of the treatments successfully alleviated his physical suffering, and the endless cycle of failed attempts eventually led to deep depression—a common consequence for those trapped in relentless pain with no end in sight.

Connick’s story, however, offers a powerful testament to the impact of modern medical innovation. His long struggle finally ended when he received an implanted peripheral nerve stimulator. The targeted device successfully disrupted the pain signals, providing Connick with the relief that had eluded him for over half a decade. 

While Connick’s outcome highlights the life-changing potential of advanced pain-management technologies, it also underscores a pressing need in modern medicine. Closing the educational gaps in healthcare and expanding access to specialized treatments are critical steps toward ensuring that the millions of Americans living in silence with chronic pain can finally find lasting relief.

**Rewiring Pain: How an Innovative Bioelectronic Device Restored One Man’s Life After Six Years of Agony**

For six long years, Timothy Connick’s world was defined by a single, unrelenting reality: severe, excruciating pain. What began as a localized issue escalated into a debilitating, chronic condition that turned everyday tasks—sitting at a desk, taking a walk, or even enjoying a full night’s sleep—into formidable hurdles. Like millions of others caught in the grip of chronic pain, Connick found himself cycling through a battery of standard treatments. He tried physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, and targeted injections, yet nothing brought meaningful or lasting relief. 

Connick’s experience is far from unique. In the United States, chronic pain is a quiet epidemic, affecting an estimated 50 million adults. For a significant portion of these individuals, the pain is "refractory"—meaning it resists conventional pharmaceuticals and traditional interventions. While the opioid crisis demonstrated the dangers of over-relying on heavy pain medications, the alternative for many patients has been a barren landscape of limited options and dead ends. Furthermore, the American healthcare system remains notoriously ill-equipped to address chronic pain holistically. Patients frequently face fragmented care, dismissal from medical providers who struggle to diagnose invisible suffering, and tedious insurance battles over advanced therapies.

Desperate for a solution after six years of relentless agony, Connick turned to a specialized medical team that proposed an innovative approach: a peripheral nerve stimulator (PNS). 

Unlike traditional spinal cord stimulators, which target nerves along the central spine, a peripheral nerve stimulator is implanted directly near the specific peripheral nerves responsible for transmitting pain signals from a targeted region of the body. In Connick’s case, doctors performed a minimally invasive procedure to implant a tiny, wire-like device just above his hip. 

The mechanism behind the technology is both precise and elegant. The implanted device delivers mild electrical pulses directly to the targeted peripheral nerve. These tiny electrical shocks do not harm the body; instead, they essentially "scramble" or block the pain signals traveling along the nerve pathway before they can reach the brain. Rather than feeling sharp, excruciating pain, the patient feels either nothing at all or a gentle, pleasant tingling sensation known as paresthesia.

For Connick, the results were transformative. Almost immediately following the activation of the device, the debilitating pain that had anchored him for over half a decade receded. The successful intervention provided him with the relief he had spent six agonizing years searching for, allowing him to reclaim his mobility, his independence, and his quality of life.

Timothy Connick’s story highlights a crucial turning point in modern medicine. As field-defining advancements in bioelectronic medicine continue to emerge, devices like peripheral nerve stimulators offer a beacon of hope for millions of suffering Americans. **'A Pacemaker for Pain': How Peripheral Nerve Stimulators Are Offering Drug-Free Relief to Millions**

**CHICAGO —** For more than five years, 58-year-old Mark Benson couldn’t walk more than a few blocks without excruciating, burning pain shooting down his right leg. Following a severe bout of shingles and a subsequent knee surgery, Benson was left with chronic neuropathic pain that refused to yield to physical therapy, steroid injections, or heavy prescription painkillers. 

"I was trapped in my own body," Benson said. "The meds made me foggy, and the pain made me miserable."

Then, six months ago, Benson underwent a 30-minute, minimally invasive procedure to implant a device known as a Peripheral Nerve Stimulator (PNS). Today, he says his pain has dropped by nearly 80 percent, and he is back to hiking with his grandchildren—without taking a single pain pill.

Benson is part of a growing wave of patients benefiting from modern Peripheral Nerve Stimulation, a fast-advancing field of medical technology that experts say is revolutionizing the management of severe chronic pain.

### How It Works: "Rewiring" the Pain Signal

Often described as a "pacemaker for nerves," a PNS system uses miniature technology to interrupt pain signals before they ever reach the brain. 

During the outpatient procedure, a physician uses ultrasound or X-ray guidance to place a tiny, thread-like wire (a lead) next to the specific peripheral nerve responsible for the patient's pain—whether in the shoulder, knee, lower back, foot, or arm. 

Once implanted, the device delivers tiny electrical pulses to the nerve. These pulses replace the sharp, agonizing pain sensations with a gentle, often unnoticeable tingling, or simply neutralize the pain entirely. 

"Think of the nerve as a telephone line sending a distress signal to the brain," said Dr. Elena Rostova, a leading interventional pain specialist in Chicago. "The stimulator essentially creates 'static' on the line. The brain never receives the pain message, so the patient doesn't feel it."

While spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has been used for decades to treat broad back and leg pain, PNS focuses specifically on individual nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. This precise targeting makes it ideal for localized pain stemming from nerve injuries, joint replacements, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), or chronic post-surgical pain.

### A Weapon Against the Opioid Crisis

The rise of PNS technology comes at a crucial moment. With the ongoing national opioid epidemic, both doctors and patients are desperately seeking non-addictive, non-pharmacological alternatives for long-term pain management.

"Opioids mask pain, but they come with severe risks of dependency, tolerance, and debilitating side effects," Dr. Rostova explained. "PNS offers a targeted, drug-free alternative that addresses the underlying neural mechanism of pain without altering a patient's brain chemistry or clarity."

Furthermore, modern PNS devices are vastly superior to their predecessors. Historically, peripheral nerve stimulation required open, invasive surgery to expose the nerve. Today’s devices are implanted using a needle, leaving behind only a tiny bandage. 

Some newer PNS systems are designed for short-term use—worn for just 60 days—to "retrain" the nervous system and provide long-lasting pain relief even after the device is removed. Others are fully internal, powered wirelessly or by tiny rechargeable batteries implanted under the skin for long-term use.

### Life-Changing Results, But Accessibility Remains a Hurdle

Clinical studies on modern PNS systems show remarkable results. Recent clinical trials published in major pain management journals indicate that over 70% to 80% of carefully selected patients experience significant pain reduction—defined as a 50% or greater decrease in pain—along with marked improvements in physical function and sleep quality.

Despite its success, challenges remain. PNS is not a universal cure; it requires careful patient screening to ensure the pain is originating from a specific, targeted peripheral nerve. 

Additionally, navigating insurance coverage can still be a hurdle for some patients. While Medicare and many major private insurers now cover PNS for specific conditions, obtaining prior authorization can sometimes be a lengthy process. Medical societies are currently working to update coverage guidelines to reflect the rapid advancements in the technology.

### A Hopeful Future

For patients like Mark Benson, the technology has delivered something that felt lost forever: a normal life.

"When you’re in severe pain every second of the day, you lose your quality of life," Benson said, holding up the small external remote he uses to adjust the stimulation levels of his device. "This little piece of technology didn't just fix my pain—it gave me my life back."

As technology continues to miniaturize and clinical evidence mounts, experts predict that Peripheral Nerve Stimulation will soon shift from a "last resort" treatment to a frontline therapy for severe chronic pain, offering hope to millions who thought they were out of options.

**ATLANTA (CNN) —** To look at 42-year-old Sarah Miller, you would never know she was living in a burning house. 

She wasn't surrounded by smoke or flames, but inside her body, a localized inferno was raging. For nearly six years, a sharp, searing pain traveled down her lower back and into her right leg—a sensation Sarah describes as "liquid fire mixed with electric shocks."

Yet, doctor after doctor told her the same frustrating sentence: *“Your X-rays and MRIs look completely normal.”*

Sarah’s story is far from unique. It represents a quiet, agonizing epidemic in modern medicine: chronic, undiagnosed nerve damage. For millions of Americans, the road to a correct diagnosis is a demoralizing marathon of misdirections, canceled plans, and invisible torment.

"The hardest part wasn't just the physical agony," Sarah told us, her voice shaking slightly as she recalled those dark years. "It was the isolation. When tests come back clean, people—sometimes even doctors—start to look at you like it’s all in your head. You begin to question your own sanity."

### The Invisible Injury

Nerve injuries are notoriously difficult to pinpoint. Unlike a broken bone or a torn ligament, damaged or malfunctioning nerves often leave no visible trail on standard imaging scans. A routine surgical procedure, a minor fender bender, or even a deep bruise can stretch or entrap microscopic nerve fibers, causing them to send continuous, frantic pain signals to the brain.

According to pain management specialists, the average chronic nerve pain patient suffers for three to five years and sees up to four different doctors before receiving an accurate diagnosis.

"Nerves are the electrical wiring of the human body," explains Dr. Aris Thorne, a neurologist and interventional pain specialist at Emory University Hospital. "When a wire is frayed, it sparks. But traditional imaging doesn't always show us the fraying—it only shows us the wall the wire is hidden inside. Because of this, patients are frequently misdiagnosed with general back strain or emotional distress, delaying proper care for years."

By the time patients finally learn the true culprit—neuropathic pain caused by peripheral nerve damage—the chronic pain has often reshaped their lives, leading to job loss, severe depression, and fractured personal relationships.

### A High-Tech Interception

For years, the standard treatment for chronic nerve pain relied heavily on high-dose prescription opioids or heavy anti-seizure medications, which often came with debilitating side effects and varying degrees of success. 

Today, however, a quiet revolution in medical technology is offering renewed hope: spinal cord and peripheral nerve stimulation. 

Often described as a "pacemaker for pain," an implanted spinal cord stimulator is a tiny, battery-powered device surgically placed beneath the skin. Thin, flexible wires (leads) are positioned in the epidural space near the spinal cord or directly adjacent to the damaged peripheral nerve. 

Instead of allowing the misfiring nerve to send pain messages to the brain, the stimulator emits mild electrical pulses. These pulses intercept the pain signals, replacing the searing agony with a gentle tingling sensation known as paresthesia—or, in newer "burst" models, no sensation at all, just sweet relief.

"It doesn't cure the underlying nerve damage," Dr. Thorne notes. "But it changes the way the brain perceives it. It turns down the volume of the pain from a deafening roar to a manageable whisper."

### "I Got My Life Back"

Before commitment to permanent surgery, patients undergo a "trial run." A temporary stimulator is taped to the outside of the body for a week while the leads are positioned under the skin. 

For Sarah, the trial week was nothing short of miraculous. 

"Within two hours of turning the device on, the burning stopped," Sarah said, smiling through tears. "For the first time in six years, I sat on the floor and played a board game with my children. I wept."

Following a successful trial, Sarah underwent a minor, minimally invasive surgery to permanently implant the device in her upper buttocks, with controls managed via a smartphone application. Today, she estimates her pain has been reduced by nearly 80 percent. She has returned to work part-time and recently went on her first family hike in nearly a decade.

### The Message to Patients

While neurostimulation isn't a silver bullet for every patient, experts stress that its success underscores a crucial message for those still trapped in the dark room of undiagnosed pain: do not give up. 

Medical technology is evolving rapidly, and interventional pain specialists are developing increasingly sophisticated ways to trace and treat the body’s complex wiring. 

"If you are living with unexplained, burning, or shooting pain, know that your pain is real," Sarah says, looking directly into the camera. "Keep fighting. Keep asking questions. The right doctor, and the right technology, are out there."

For CNN Medical News, I’m Judy Fortin, reporting.

**BOSTON —** For six long years, Mark Miller’s world was defined by a relentless, burning agony in his lower back and right leg. 

It began in 2018 after what seemed like a minor slip on an icy sidewalk. But while the bruising faded, the pain grew, eventually turning the former 42-year-old high school physical education teacher into a bedridden spectator in his own life.

Over the next half-decade, Miller saw nearly a dozen specialists. He was diagnosed with everything from muscle strain and degenerative disc disease to phantom pain. He underwent twice-weekly physical therapy, endured painful steroid injections, and was prescribed increasingly potent opioids that left him in a mental fog. At one point, a doctor gently suggested his pain might be psychological.

“I felt like I was losing my mind,” Miller recalled. “The pain was an 8 out of 10 every single day. I couldn’t work, I couldn’t play with my kids, and nobody could tell me why.”

It wasn't until late last year, when Miller was referred to Dr. Aris Thorne, a neurologist at the Boston Neurological Institute, that the trajectory of his life finally changed.

### The Missing Diagnosis

Dr. Thorne took a different approach, looking beyond the structural MRI scans that previous doctors had focused on. Instead of looking for bone or disc abnormalities, Thorne conducted a comprehensive neurological evaluation, including an electromyogram (EMG) and nerve conduction studies, to measure the electrical activity of Miller’s nerves.

The result was immediate and definitive: Miller wasn't suffering from a bad back. He had severe, localized nerve damage—specifically, chronic neuropathic pain caused by an entrapment and inflammation of the sciatic nerve branch, which had gone undetected on standard imaging.

“Mark’s brain was receiving continuous, frantic 'fire alarm' signals from damaged nerves that were firing uncontrollably,” Dr. Thorne explained. “Because his structural spine looked relatively normal, previous clinicians missed the fact that the electrical wiring itself was broken.”

Diagnosing the problem, however, was only half the battle. After six years, the nerve pathways had wired themselves to perpetually transmit pain. Traditional medications were no longer effective.

### Borrowing from Cardiac Medicine

To fix the electrical problem, Dr. Thorne turned to a solution rooted in cardiology: a specialized device built on the same core technology as a heart pacemaker. 

Known as a Spinal Cord Stimulator (SCS), the device consists of a tiny battery-powered generator implanted under the skin and thin insulated wires (leads) placed near the spinal cord. Just as a cardiac pacemaker delivers small electrical pulses to keep a heart beating in rhythm, the SCS delivers mild electrical signals directly to the spinal cord. 

These electrical impulses intercept the pain signals traveling from damaged peripheral nerves before they can reach the brain. Instead of feeling sharp, burning pain, the patient feels either a gentle tingling sensation—known as paresthesia—or, with newer high-frequency devices, no sensation at all, just the absence of pain.

“It is essentially a pacemaker for the nervous system,” said Dr. Thorne. “Instead of regulating a heartbeat, we are overriding faulty electrical signals in the pain pathways.”

### A Second Chance at Life

In November, Miller underwent a one-week trial with a temporary, external version of the device. The results were instantaneous.

“Within two hours of turning it on, my pain dropped by 80 percent,” Miller said, holding back tears. “For the first time in six years, I took a deep breath without aching.”

Following the successful trial, a permanent device—roughly the size of a silver dollar—was surgically implanted in Miller’s upper buttock during a minor, outpatient procedure.

Today, six months after the surgery, Miller is off all prescription pain medications. He has returned to part-time teaching, coaches his daughter’s soccer team, and recently completed his first 5K walk. Using a smartphone app, he can adjust the device's electrical settings depending on his activity level.

For Miller, the device represents far more than just medical innovation.

“I spent six years in the dark, being told I had to live with it,” Miller said. “This technology didn’t just mask my pain—it gave me my family, my career, and my life back.”
